title: Water Cell Farthest From Any Shore
statement:
You get an n × n grid where 1 is land and 0 is water. The distance between cells (r1, c1) and (r2, c2) is |r1 − r2| + |c1 − c2|.

For each water cell, look at its distance to the nearest land cell. Return the largest of these values over all water cells. If the grid has no land or no water at all, return -1.

examples.why: The only land is the top-right corner. The bottom-left water cell is 2 rows and 2 columns away from it.
The top-right corner is 2 away from both land cells. What counts is the nearest land, not the farthest one, so 4 would be wrong.
There is no water cell to measure.

hints: Running a search from every water cell to find its nearest land repeats a lot of work. Can you start the search from the other side?
Start a breadth-first search from all land cells at once. The first time the search reaches a water cell, that is its distance to the nearest land.
Put every land cell in the queue at distance 0 and expand one ring at a time. The ring number of the last water cell reached is the answer. With no land or no water, return -1 up front.

explain.intuition:
Picture the land flooding outward one step per minute, in four directions. A water cell gets reached at the minute equal to its distance from the nearest land, because whichever land is closest gets there first. The answer is the minute when the last water cell is reached.

That flooding is a breadth-first search with many starting points: put every land cell in the queue at once. Each cell enters the queue once, so the cost is O(n²) for the whole grid instead of O(n²) per water cell. On a 4-neighbour grid with no obstacles, BFS steps are exactly Manhattan distance.
steps: Push every land cell into a queue. If the queue is empty or holds all n² cells, return -1.
Process the queue level by level. For each cell, look at its four neighbours.
A neighbour that is still water is reached now: mark it as visited (for example set it to 1 in a copy) and push it.
Count the levels. When the queue runs dry, the number of levels that reached new water is the answer.
pitfalls: Taking the distance to the farthest land instead of the nearest one. The second example shows the difference.
Running a separate BFS from each water cell or each land cell. That is O(n⁴) on a 100 × 100 grid.
Marking cells visited when they are popped instead of when they are pushed, so a cell enters the queue several times.

solutions.title: Check every water–land pair
solutions.idea: For each water cell, compute the distance to every land cell and keep the minimum. The answer is the largest minimum.

solutions.title: Multi-source BFS from all land
solutions.idea: Flood outward from every land cell at once. The number of rings needed to cover all water is the answer.

solutions.title: Two sweeps of DP
solutions.idea: The nearest land is reached by going up/left or down/right first. One sweep from the top-left and one from the bottom-right compute every distance.

followups: Some cells are rocks that the flood cannot cross. Which of the two fast methods still works?
Return the coordinates of every water cell that reaches the maximum, not just the distance.
